On the original model the top prediction should nearly always match the model's own greedy text, so escape and divergence rates should be close to zero. If they aren't, my alignment is wrong. For each text I'll count whether the top choice departs from the actual token anywhere in the first repetition (loops), or anywhere in the answer (controls).

Then I'll set up the first candidate, E12: removing both L5 pointer heads, h2 and h3, by zeroing their `o_proj` columns. I'm starting with the strongest L5 test because it decides the most at once. If removing both doesn't let answers escape, L5 h3 alone can't either, which saves a pass. The expected good outcome is a loop escape rate well above baseline, by more than 10 points, with a clearly lower divergence rate on correct answers. If those rise together, L5 has no selective role in looping.

Tiny numerical differences between batches mean that "any mismatch" happens in 38% of correct answers even with no edit, so that metric is noisy for long texts. I'll treat per-token mismatch (baseline 0.29%) as the main damage measure, alongside the first-repeat escape rate (baseline 4.9%).

E12 is saved with both L5 pointer heads zeroed, which removes 37% of that layer's head output energy. The notes are current, so this is the first screen.

Logprobs fell only slightly across the texts, so the model hasn't broken, but that doesn't say whether the edit is selective. Now the screen itself: I'll compare loop escape with per-token mismatch on correct and wrong answers, against pass 35. I'm also adding the escape latency, since an escape early in the first repeat would be more useful than one near its end. I need to read this carefully, because the headline is misleading. Escape jumped from 4.9% to 65.9% (126 new, 1 lost), which looks like a loop fix. But per-token mismatch rose tenfold everywhere, from 0.29% to 2.97% on correct answers and to 4.19% on wrong ones. At about 3% per token, a 50-token repeat would show at least one mismatch roughly 78% of the time by chance alone. So a 66% "escape" may be nothing more than general perturbation. The logprob of copied tokens fell only 0.028, which also suggests copying is barely touched. My any-mismatch metric saturates, as I noted for the controls, and I shouldn't have compared it with per-token damage.

The fair comparison uses the same unit on both sides: per-token mismatch inside the first repeat, against per-token mismatch on correct and wrong answers. A selective loop edit should change copied tokens at a clearly higher rate than ordinary tokens. If the first-repeat rate is about the same or lower, E12 has no loop selectivity and is just a broad perturbation.
